content.summary: Basic Calculator: A basic calculator helps us compute numbers accurately. It matters in shopping, measuring, and checking homework.
content.explanation: Use this lesson as a small experiment. Arithmetic expressions may contain several operations. Brackets decide what happens first. Without brackets, multiplication and division happen before addition and subtraction. A common mistake is solving from left to right every time. Enter the expression. Check brackets first. Evaluate powers if present. Then multiply or divide from left to right. Finally add or subtract from left to right. These rules keep one expression from having many different answers.

content.summary: Natural Numbers: Natural numbers are the numbers we use for counting. They start at 1 and keep going forever. We use them when counting books, steps, seats, or people.
content.explanation: Use this lesson as a small experiment. The basic idea is one more. After 1 comes 2, after 2 comes 3, and this never stops. On a number line, natural numbers sit to the right of zero as equally spaced marks. A basket with 5 apples shows the natural number 5. A classroom with 28 students shows 28. Page 12 in a book also uses a natural number. Zero is not included in this lesson's convention, because zero means none, not one counted object. Fractions such as 1/2 are not natural numbers because they do not count whole objects. A common mistake is saying every number is natural. Negative numbers, decimals, fractions, and zero do not belong to this set here. Choose a counting number. Move right by one equal step to get its successor. Compare two natural numbers by checking which one is farther right. Counting works by matching one number name to one object. Equal number-line spacing keeps the order exact.

content.summary: Rational Numbers: Rational numbers are numbers that can be written as a fraction. The denominator cannot be zero. They help us compare parts, money, measurements, and exact ratios.
content.explanation: Use this lesson as a small experiment. A rational number is any number that can be written as a/b, where a and b are integers and b is not 0. So 3/4, -5/2, 0, and 7 are rational numbers. The whole number 7 is rational because it can be written as 7/1. The decimal 0.25 is rational because it equals 1/4. A price of 3.50 rupees, half a litre, and a score of 2 out of 5 are rational quantities. Rational numbers work because division by a non-zero whole number creates an exact ratio. A common mistake is thinking only proper fractions are rational. Whole numbers, negative fractions, and terminating or repeating decimals are rational too. Write the number as a fraction with integer numerator and non-zero integer denominator. Then place its value on the number line. The denominator sets equal parts of one unit, so the fraction gives an exact location or comparison.

content.summary: Irrational Numbers: Irrational numbers are real numbers that cannot be written as exact fractions of integers. Their decimals do not end or repeat. They appear in lengths, circles, and square roots.
content.explanation: Use this lesson as a small experiment. An irrational number cannot be written as a/b, where a and b are integers and b is not 0. Its decimal form goes on forever without a repeating block. Examples include sqrt(2), sqrt(3), and pi. The diagonal of a square with side 1 has length sqrt(2), which is irrational. A circle's circumference uses pi. Some scientific measurements use irrational values before rounding. The reason these numbers are needed is that rational numbers do not fill every point on the number line. A common mistake is thinking a long decimal is always irrational. A decimal like 0.3333... repeats, so it is rational. Check whether the number can be written as an exact fraction. Non-ending, non-repeating decimals are irrational. Some geometric lengths and constants cannot be expressed as a ratio of two integers.

content.summary: Real Numbers: Real numbers fill the number line. They include whole numbers, integers, fractions, decimals, and irrational numbers. We use them for nearly every measurement in school mathematics.
content.explanation: Use this lesson as a small experiment. A real number is any rational or irrational number on the number line. Integers like -4, fractions like 2/3, decimals like 1.5, and irrational numbers like sqrt(2) are real. Real numbers can describe height, distance, temperature, money, and time. A runner's time of 12.8 seconds is real. A temperature of -3 degrees is real. The length pi cm is real, even if we use an approximation. Real numbers work as one big system for measuring continuous quantities. A common mistake is thinking real means only numbers we can write exactly as decimals. Irrational numbers are real too, even when their decimals never end or repeat. Place rational and irrational values on one shared number line. Compare them by position. The real number system combines exact ratios and non-ratio lengths into one ordered line.

content.summary: Prime Numbers: Prime numbers are building-block numbers. They have exactly two positive factors. They matter in factorisation, fractions, codes, and number patterns.
content.explanation: Use this lesson as a small experiment. A prime number is greater than 1 and has exactly two positive factors: 1 and itself. The number 2 is prime because its only positive factors are 1 and 2. The number 9 is not prime because 1, 3, and 9 divide it. Prime numbers include 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, and 13. They help break numbers into prime factors. Packaging 13 items gives only 1 by 13 equal rectangle. Computer security uses very large primes. Fraction simplification uses prime factors. A common mistake is saying 1 is prime. It has only one positive factor, so it is not prime. Check divisors from 2 up to the square root. If none divide the number and it is greater than 1, it is prime. A composite number must have a factor pair, and one factor in the pair is at most the square root.

content.summary: Divisibility Rules: Divisibility rules are shortcuts for exact division. They help us test numbers without doing long division every time. We use them when simplifying fractions, finding factors, and checking mental arithmetic.
content.explanation: Use this lesson as a small experiment. A number is divisible by another number when division leaves remainder 0. Divisibility rules use place value to test this quickly. A number is divisible by 2 if its last digit is even. It is divisible by 5 if its last digit is 0 or 5. It is divisible by 10 if its last digit is 0. For 3, add the digits; 123 is divisible by 3 because 1 + 2 + 3 = 6, and 6 is divisible by 3. These rules help check classroom groups, packet counts, and fraction simplification. They work because base-ten place values have predictable remainders. A common mistake is using a rule for the wrong divisor, such as testing divisibility by 9 with only the last digit. Choose the divisor. Apply only its matching rule. Confirm by checking that the remainder is 0 when needed. Place value lets the same remainders repeat, so a shortcut can replace full division.

content.summary: Modular Arithmetic: Modular arithmetic is arithmetic with remainders. It is like counting around a clock. We use it for time, repeating patterns, calendar days, and computer checks.
content.explanation: Use this lesson as a small experiment. In modular arithmetic, we care about the remainder after division by a fixed number called the modulus. On a 12-hour clock, 15 hours after 0 lands at 3 because 15 leaves remainder 3 when divided by 12. We write 15 congruent to 3 modulo 12. If today is Monday, 10 days later is Thursday because 10 leaves remainder 3 after groups of 7 days. Modular arithmetic works for clock times, calendars, repeating colour patterns, and barcode checks. It works because values that differ by a whole number of cycles land in the same position. A common mistake is giving the quotient instead of the remainder. In mod 5, 17 gives remainder 2, not quotient 3. Divide by the modulus. Keep the remainder. Use that remainder as the position in the cycle. Adding or subtracting full cycles does not change the final position in the repeating pattern.

content.summary: Continued Fractions: A continued fraction is a nested fraction. It gives good rational approximations to numbers. We use it in number theory, approximation, and pattern study.
content.explanation: Use this lesson as a small experiment. A continued fraction writes a number as a whole part plus a reciprocal, then repeats this idea inside the denominator. For example, 3 + 1/2 is a short continued fraction for 3.5. A longer one looks like 1 + 1/(2 + 1/3). Continued fractions can approximate irrational numbers with fractions that are often very accurate. They help estimate roots, compare rational approximations, and study patterns in numbers. They work because each added layer improves the approximation while keeping a fraction form. A common mistake is flattening the nested fraction too early and losing the denominator structure. Each reciprocal layer must be evaluated from the inside outward. Start with the innermost fraction. Evaluate one reciprocal layer at a time until the whole expression is complete. Nested reciprocals create a sequence of rational approximations called convergents.

content.summary: Equivalent Fractions: Equivalent fractions look different but show the same amount. They are useful for comparing, adding, and simplifying fractions. We see them in recipes, measurements, and sharing.
content.explanation: Use this lesson as a small experiment. Equivalent fractions have the same value. For example, 1/2, 2/4, and 3/6 all name the same amount. Rs 50 out of Rs 100 is the same as 1/2 of the money. A measuring cup marked 2/4 is the same as 1/2. This works because the part count and part size change together. A common mistake is changing only the numerator or only the denominator. That changes the value. Multiply or divide numerator and denominator by the same non-zero factor. content.summary: Decimal Place Value: Decimal place value tells what digits after the decimal point mean. It helps us read money, measurements, and scores. Each step right is one tenth of the previous place.
content.explanation: Use this lesson as a small experiment. In 3.47, the 3 is ones, the 4 is tenths, and the 7 is hundredths. So 3.47 means 3 + 4/10 + 7/100. Decimal places keep dividing by 10 as we move right. Money uses decimal place value: Rs 12.50 means 12 rupees and 50 paise if two decimal places are used. A length of 1.25 m means 1 metre and 25 hundredths of a metre. A race time of 9.8 seconds uses tenths. Decimal place value works because base ten continues past the ones place. A common mistake is thinking 0.5 is smaller than 0.47 because 5 has fewer digits. Actually 0.50 is greater than 0.47. Name each place from the decimal point: tenths, hundredths, thousandths. Add trailing zeros only to compare, not to change value. Each decimal place is one tenth of the place to its left.

The value 0.333 is only an approximation to 1/3, not the exact same number. Divide numerator by denominator. Watch the remainder. If a remainder repeats, the decimal block repeats. Long division has only finitely many possible remainders, so a repeated remainder creates repeated digits.

content.summary: Unit Rates: A unit rate tells how much for one. It helps compare prices, speeds, and work rates. We use it when choosing the better buy or reading speed.
content.explanation: Use this lesson as a small experiment. A unit rate is a rate with the second quantity equal to 1. If 5 kg of rice costs 300 rupees, the unit rate is 300/5 = 60 rupees per kg. If a car travels 180 km in 3 hours, its speed is 60 km per hour. Unit rates help compare shop prices, internet speed, fuel use, and wages. They work because dividing by the number of units gives the amount for one unit. A common mistake is reversing the division. For rupees per kilogram, divide rupees by kilograms, not kilograms by rupees. Identify the quantity wanted per one unit. Divide the first amount by the matching number of units. Division shares the total evenly across each single unit.

content.summary: Percentages: A percentage is a way to say out of 100. The word percent means per hundred. We use percentages for marks, discounts, battery charge, tax, and sports scores.
content.explanation: Use this lesson as a small experiment. 25% means 25 out of 100 equal parts. As a fraction, it is 25/100. As a decimal, it is 0.25. A phone battery at 80% has 80 out of 100 parts filled. A test score of 45% means 45 marks out of every 100 marks. A 10% discount removes 10 rupees from each 100 rupees of price. Percentages work because using 100 as a common whole makes comparisons easy. A common mistake is treating 25% as 25 in multiplication. For finding 25% of 80, use 25/100 x 80, not 25 x 80. Write the percent number over 100. Divide by 100 for decimal form. Multiply the decimal by the whole to find that percent of an amount. Percentages use the same-size base of 100, so different quantities can be compared fairly.

content.summary: Percentage Change: Percentage change measures increase or decrease compared with the original amount. It is common in discounts, marks, prices, and population changes.
content.explanation: Use this lesson as a small experiment. Percentage change is change divided by original amount, then multiplied by 100. If a price rises from 80 to 100, the change is 20. The percentage increase is 20/80 x 100 = 25%. If a shirt drops from 500 to 400 rupees, the change is -100, so the decrease is 20%. Percentage change helps read sales, exam improvement, sports records, and data reports. It works because the original amount is the base for comparison. A common mistake is dividing by the new amount. For percentage change, always compare the change with the original amount. Find new minus original. Divide by original. Multiply by 100 and name increase or decrease. Using the original amount as the base makes changes from different sizes comparable.

content.summary: Compound Change: Compound change means repeated percentage increase or decrease. Each step uses the new amount, not the starting amount. We see it in growth, depreciation, and compound interest.
content.explanation: Use this lesson as a small experiment. In compound change, each percentage change is applied to the current amount. A 10% increase has multiplier 1.10. Starting from 100, one increase gives 110. A second 10% increase gives 121, not 120, because it uses 10% of 110. Compound decrease works the same way with a multiplier less than 1, such as 0.9 for a 10% decrease. It appears in population growth, phone value depreciation, investments, and repeated discounts. It works because each step creates a new base. A common mistake is adding the same percentage of the original each time. That is simple change, not compound change. Convert the percentage to a multiplier. Multiply the current amount once for each period. Every period changes the base, so growth or decrease builds on the latest value.

Repeated discounts: Each discount uses the reduced price.

content.summary: Scale Drawings: A scale drawing is a smaller or larger drawing of a real object. It keeps the same shape by scaling every length equally. We use it in maps, floor plans, models, and designs.
content.explanation: Use this lesson as a small experiment. In a scale drawing, all lengths are multiplied by the same scale factor. If 1 cm on a map represents 5 km, then 3 cm represents 15 km. A room plan might use 1 cm for 1 metre. A toy car model might use 1:20 scale. Scale drawings help architects, map readers, engineers, and students work with large or small objects on paper. They work because multiplying every length by the same factor preserves shape and angle size. A common mistake is scaling one length but not another. That changes the shape and makes the drawing inaccurate. Read the scale. Multiply drawing length by the real-length factor, or divide real length by the factor for drawing length. Equal scaling preserves proportional lengths in the drawing and the real object.

content.summary: Algebra Tiles: Algebra tiles turn expressions into visible pieces. They help students see adding, subtracting, and factoring. Builders, budget planners, and coders all use this same idea of parts making a whole.
content.explanation: Use this lesson as a small experiment. A tile for x is an unknown length. A unit tile is 1. A group like 3x + 2 means three x tiles and two unit tiles. The model works because equal tiles represent equal algebraic values. A common mistake is joining unlike tiles, such as x and 1, as if their sizes match. Match each symbol to its tile. Combine only identical tiles. Use zero pairs to remove opposite tiles. Only like-shaped tiles have the same value, so only they can be combined.

content.summary: Like Terms: Like terms are terms that can be collected together. This keeps algebra shorter and clearer. We use it when simplifying bills, formulas, and repeated unknown amounts.
content.explanation: Use this lesson as a small experiment. In 4x + 2x, both terms have x, so they combine to 6x. In 4x + 2, the parts are different, so they cannot combine. Like terms must have the same variable and the same exponent. We see like terms in monthly fees, repeated lengths, and spreadsheet formulas. This works because the coefficient counts how many identical variable parts we have. A common mistake is combining x and x squared. They are different powers, so they are not like terms. Group terms with the same variable part. Add or subtract their coefficients. Keep unlike terms separate. The distributive law says ax + bx = (a + b)x.

content.summary: Algebraic Fractions: Algebraic fractions are fractions with variables. They behave like numerical fractions, but restrictions matter. We use them in formula rearranging, rates, graphs, and rational expressions.
content.explanation: Use this lesson as a small experiment. An algebraic fraction has an expression in its numerator or denominator, such as (x + 1)/(x - 2). The denominator cannot be zero, so x cannot be 2 in this example. You simplify algebraic fractions by factoring and cancelling common factors, not common terms. For example, (x^2 - 1)/(x - 1) = (x - 1)(x + 1)/(x - 1), so it simplifies to x + 1, with x not equal to 1. Algebraic fractions appear in speed formulas, graph equations, and rates. They work because equivalent fractions keep the same value where both expressions are defined. A common mistake is cancelling across addition, such as cancelling x in (x + 2)/x. Factor numerator and denominator. State excluded values. Cancel only common factors. Keep restrictions after simplifying. Cancelling is valid only when a whole common factor is multiplied in numerator and denominator.

On a graph, the solution is where two lines meet. This is used to find two item prices, balance mixtures, and compare cost plans. It works because the same x and y must make both equations true. A common mistake is solving one equation and ignoring the other. Choose elimination or substitution. Remove one variable. Solve for the other. Substitute back and check both equations. The solution is the common point shared by both linear equations.

content.summary: Polynomial Inequalities: Polynomial inequalities extend sign testing to higher-degree expressions. They are used in graph regions, design limits, and motion models. They help find where a formula is positive or negative.
content.explanation: Use this lesson as a small experiment. For (x - 1)(x - 3)(x + 2) >= 0, the critical points are -2, 1, and 3. These split the number line into intervals. Test one value in each interval to decide the sign. This works because a polynomial can change sign only at roots with odd multiplicity. A common mistake is ignoring a repeated root, where the sign may touch and not cross. Factor the polynomial. Mark all roots. Test each interval. Include roots when the sign allows equality. Polynomial signs stay steady between roots because no factor changes sign there.

content.summary: Two-Variable Inequalities: Two-variable inequalities show all points that satisfy a rule. They are useful for budgets, planning, and map regions. A graph makes the whole answer visible.
content.explanation: Use this lesson as a small experiment. The inequality y < 2x + 1 includes points below the line y = 2x + 1. The boundary line is dashed because points on it are not included. If the sign were <=, the line would be solid. We see this in cost limits, delivery zones, and design constraints. It works because every point has x and y values that can be tested. A common mistake is shading the wrong side of the boundary. Draw the boundary line. Decide if it is solid or dashed. Test one point. Shade the side that makes the inequality true. The boundary separates points that satisfy the inequality from points that do not.

content.summary: Systems of Inequalities: Systems of inequalities show a shared region. They are used in planning, business, diet problems, and design limits. The answer must satisfy every condition.

A common mistake is keeping points that satisfy only one inequality. Graph each inequality. Use solid or dashed boundaries correctly. Keep only the overlapping shaded region. The solution set is the intersection of all individual solution regions.

content.summary: Numerical Solver: A numerical solver helps find answers by approximation. It is useful for complicated equations, models, and checking graphs. It should still be checked.
content.explanation: Use this lesson as a small experiment. If an equation is hard to solve exactly, a numerical solver searches for a value that makes the two sides nearly equal. For example, it can estimate where x^3 - x - 1 = 0. We see this in engineering models, finance calculations, and graph intersections. It works by testing values and improving the guess. A common mistake is trusting an approximate answer without checking the original equation. Choose an interval or starting guess. Let the solver improve the value. Substitute the result back to check the error. Approximation works by making the difference between both sides very small.

content.summary: Function Concept: A function is a rule from inputs to outputs. It helps describe change in graphs, tables, and formulas. We use functions for prices, travel, and machine rules.
content.explanation: Use this lesson as a small experiment. In a function, one input cannot have two different outputs. The rule f(x)=2x+1 gives one answer for each x. If x=3, the output is 7. A vending machine code, a taxi fare rule, and a temperature conversion all act like functions. This works because a clear rule must give a dependable output. A common mistake is allowing one input to point to two outputs. Choose an input. Apply the rule once. Check that the input gives only one output. Functions are reliable because each allowed input has a single assigned output.

content.summary: Domain and Range: Domain and range tell where a function can start and end. They matter in graphs and real situations. They stop us from using impossible values.

Real examples include time, distance, and item counts, which often cannot be negative. This works because the rule may break or stop making sense outside allowed inputs. A common mistake is reading range from the x-axis instead of the y-axis. Find allowed x-values for the domain. Then find possible y-values for the range. The formula and context decide which inputs and outputs are possible.

content.summary: Vertical-Line Test: The vertical-line test tells whether a graph is a function. It is important when reading graphs. It prevents one input from having two outputs.
content.explanation: Use this lesson as a small experiment. If any vertical line crosses a graph more than once, the graph is not a function. A circle fails this test because some x-values have two y-values. A normal line passes because each x gives one y. We see this when checking paths, data plots, and relation graphs. It works because vertical lines hold x constant. A common mistake is using a horizontal line for the function test. Imagine vertical lines moving across the graph. If one line hits twice, it is not a function. A vertical line fixes one input x and counts how many outputs appear.

advanced.title: Partial Quotients
advanced.summary: Read a continued fraction as a sequence of integer choices that repeatedly zoom into the remaining error.
objectives: Convert a number into partial quotients.
Explain why each reciprocal step exposes the next integer part.
Connect finite continued fractions to rational numbers.
learn: A continued fraction records a number by peeling off its integer part, then repeating the process on the reciprocal of the fractional remainder.
The partial quotients are the integers in that recursive description.
Stopping after a partial quotient gives a rational approximation called a convergent.
explore: Use the continued fractions studio with different decimal inputs and compare how quickly the partial quotients grow.
Change a rational number slightly and notice when early partial quotients stay fixed.
Compare terminating and non-terminating patterns.
practice: Find the partial quotients for 7/5, 13/8, and 22/7.
Write [2; 1, 3] as an ordinary fraction.
Explain what a large partial quotient says about a nearby rational approximation.
assessmentPrompts: Why does taking a reciprocal reveal the next partial quotient?
How can you tell from the expansion that a number is rational?

advanced.title: Convergents
advanced.summary: Build the best successive rational estimates from a continued fraction and track their error.
objectives: Compute convergents from partial quotients.
Compare convergent error against nearby fractions.
Use numerator-denominator recurrences.
learn: Each prefix of a continued fraction produces a convergent.
Convergents alternate around the target value in many familiar irrational examples.
The recurrence p_n = a_n p_{n-1} + p_{n-2} and q_n = a_n q_{n-1} + q_{n-2} builds them efficiently.
explore: Use the studio to compare convergents for pi, sqrt(2), and the golden ratio.
Watch how denominator size and approximation error move together.
Identify which convergent gives the strongest estimate under a denominator cap.
practice: Compute the first four convergents of [1; 2, 2, 2, ...].
Find the error of 22/7 as an approximation to pi.
Choose the better approximation to sqrt(2): 7/5 or 10/7.
assessmentPrompts: Why are convergents useful when denominator size is limited?
What information is lost if you only store a decimal approximation?

advanced.title: Euclidean Algorithm Link
advanced.summary: See how gcd division steps are the same structure as a rational continued fraction.
objectives: Map Euclidean divisions to partial quotients.
Use remainders to form a finite continued fraction.
Explain why rational continued fractions terminate.
learn: For a rational number a/b, repeated division a = qb + r gives the same quotients that appear in the continued fraction.
The process terminates exactly when a remainder becomes zero.
This connects gcd computation to rational reconstruction.
explore: Enter ratios with a common factor and compare the gcd chain to the fraction expansion.
Try consecutive Fibonacci numbers and observe the long string of ones.
Reverse the quotients to rebuild the original fraction.
practice: Use Euclidean division to expand 43/19.
Explain why 34/21 has many partial quotients equal to 1.
Reconstruct a fraction from quotients 3, 4, 2.
assessmentPrompts: How does the final nonzero remainder relate to gcd?
Why do Fibonacci ratios create slow Euclidean algorithms?

advanced.title: Best Rational Approximations
advanced.summary: Use continued fractions to find fractions that beat every competitor with a smaller denominator.
objectives: Define best approximation under a denominator limit.
Use convergents as high-quality candidates.
Compare approximation error fairly.
learn: A best rational approximation balances closeness against denominator size.
Continued fraction convergents are unusually strong because they encode long-lasting integer structure.
Semi-convergents can also matter between two consecutive convergents.
explore: Search for the best fraction to approximate pi with denominators below 10, 100, and 1000.
Compare decimal rounding with continued fraction rounding.
Use error bars to see when two fractions are practically indistinguishable.
practice: Find a strong approximation to sqrt(3) with denominator below 20.
Compare 355/113 and 22/7 for pi.
Explain why a smaller absolute error is not the only criterion.
assessmentPrompts: What makes an approximation 'best' in a denominator-limited setting?
When might a semi-convergent be useful?

advanced.title: Periodic Square Roots
advanced.summary: Discover why square roots of non-square integers produce repeating continued fractions.
objectives: Recognize periodic continued fractions.
Connect quadratic irrationals to repeating expansions.
Use periods to approximate square roots.
learn: Square roots of non-square integers are quadratic irrationals.
Their continued fractions eventually repeat, and for square roots the repetition starts immediately after the integer part.
The period length carries arithmetic information about the number.
explore: Compare sqrt(2), sqrt(3), sqrt(5), and sqrt(13) in the studio.
Track the repeated block and the convergents it produces.
Use the repeated block to generate increasingly accurate approximations.
practice: Write the repeating pattern for sqrt(2).
Compute three convergents from [1; 2, 2, 2, ...].
Describe how periodicity differs from a terminating rational expansion.
assessmentPrompts: Why does a repeating continued fraction suggest a quadratic equation?
How is this like and unlike repeating decimals?

advanced.title: Collatz Conjecture
advanced.summary: Experiment with the 3n + 1 rule and distinguish evidence from proof.
objectives: Apply the Collatz rule to generate an orbit.
Track stopping time and peak value.
Explain why computation is not a proof.
learn: The rule sends even n to n/2 and odd n to 3n + 1.
The conjecture says every positive integer eventually reaches 1.
Many starting values have been tested, but a general proof remains unknown.
explore: Use the famous problems studio to compare stopping times for nearby starting values.
Look for starts with unusually high peaks.
Try grouping values by parity patterns.
practice: Compute the orbit starting at 7 until it reaches 1.
Find the first value above 10 in the orbit from 3.
Write one sentence separating verified examples from proof.
assessmentPrompts: Why does checking a million cases not settle the conjecture?
What data would make a good Collatz visualization?

advanced.title: Goldbach Conjecture
advanced.summary: Represent even numbers as sums of two primes and observe the unresolved pattern.
objectives: Test Goldbach partitions for even numbers.
Count how many prime pairs represent a value.
Explain the conjecture in precise language.
learn: The strong Goldbach conjecture states that every even integer greater than 2 is the sum of two primes.
Examples are easy to find, but the universal claim is still open.
Prime density heuristics make the pattern plausible while stopping short of proof.
explore: Use the studio to scan even numbers and count prime-pair representations.
Compare small even numbers with larger ones.
Look for symmetry in pairs p + q = n.
practice: List all Goldbach pairs for 28.
Find two prime sums for 50.
Explain why 2 is excluded from the claim.
assessmentPrompts: What would a counterexample need to look like?
Why do prime counts matter for intuition here?

advanced.title: Riemann Hypothesis and Primes
advanced.summary: Connect zeros of the zeta function to the rhythm of prime counting.
objectives: Describe the prime-counting function informally.
State the Riemann Hypothesis at a high level.
Connect zeta zeros to prime distribution error.
learn: The zeta function extends a sum over powers into complex analysis.
Its nontrivial zeros appear to lie on the critical line.
That zero pattern controls how regularly primes are distributed.
explore: Use the famous problems studio and special functions gallery together.
Compare exact prime counts with smooth approximations.
Discuss what an error term means in a counting problem.
practice: Estimate whether primes become more or less dense as numbers grow.
Name the critical line in the usual statement.
Explain why this problem bridges number theory and analysis.
assessmentPrompts: What does the hypothesis predict about prime-counting error?
Why is the zeta function surprising in a lesson about primes?

advanced.title: Fermat's Last Theorem
advanced.summary: Compare Pythagorean triples with the impossible higher-power equation.
objectives: State Fermat's Last Theorem.
Contrast exponent 2 with exponents greater than 2.
Understand why examples are not enough for impossibility.
learn: There are many whole-number solutions to a^2 + b^2 = c^2.
Fermat's Last Theorem says no positive integer solutions exist for a^n + b^n = c^n when n > 2.
The modern proof connects the statement to elliptic curves and modular forms.
explore: Search small grids for exponent 2 and exponent 3 outcomes.
Record near misses for cubes.
Use the studio to compare a conjecture, a theorem, and a proof story.
practice: Give one Pythagorean triple.
Check whether 3^3 + 4^3 is a cube.
Explain why a theorem can be true even when the proof is far beyond the lesson.
assessmentPrompts: What changes when the exponent moves from 2 to 3?
Why is 'no solutions' harder to support than 'here is one solution'?

advanced.title: Four-Color Theorem
advanced.summary: Model maps as graphs and test why four colors always suffice on a plane.
objectives: Translate a map into an adjacency graph.
Color adjacent regions with different colors.
Discuss computer-assisted proof at a learner-friendly level.
learn: The theorem says any planar map can be colored with at most four colors so neighboring regions differ.
The graph version replaces regions with vertices and borders with edges.
Its proof is famous because computers checked many unavoidable cases.
explore: Draw small maps and convert them to adjacency graphs.
Try to force a fifth color and inspect why the attempt fails.
Compare planar and nonplanar constraints.
practice: Color a five-region cycle with three colors.
Explain why touching at a single point is not usually counted as adjacency.
Name one reason the proof changed mathematical culture.
assessmentPrompts: What makes the graph planar?
Why did computer assistance matter for this theorem?

advanced.title: Confidence Intervals
advanced.summary: Interpret intervals as a repeated-sampling method rather than a guarantee about one sample.
objectives: Compute a basic confidence interval idea from estimate plus margin.
Interpret confidence level correctly.
Distinguish parameter, statistic, and interval.
learn: A confidence interval is built from sample data to estimate an unknown population parameter.
The confidence level describes long-run success of the method over repeated samples.
Wider intervals usually mean more uncertainty or higher confidence.
explore: Use the inference studio to simulate many samples and see how often intervals cover the true mean.
Change sample size and confidence level.
Compare narrow intervals with coverage.
practice: Interpret a 95% confidence interval without saying there is a 95% chance the fixed parameter lies inside.
Predict what happens when sample size quadruples.
Identify the estimate and margin of error in 42 plus or minus 3.
assessmentPrompts: What does 95% confidence mean in repeated sampling?
Why does a larger sample usually narrow the interval?

advanced.title: Margin of Error and Sample Size
advanced.summary: Control precision by connecting variability, confidence, and n.
objectives: Explain margin of error as the radius of an interval.
Describe how sample size affects precision.
Connect standard error to square-root scaling.
learn: Margin of error is the distance from the estimate to an interval endpoint.
For many common settings, standard error shrinks like 1/sqrt(n).
Doubling precision often requires about four times as much data.
explore: Move the sample-size control in the studio and watch interval width.
Hold confidence fixed, then change variability.
Compare practical precision with data-collection cost.
practice: If n grows from 25 to 100, predict the standard error change.
Explain why higher confidence widens an interval.
Find the full interval from estimate 18 and margin 2.5.
assessmentPrompts: Why does precision improve slowly as n grows?
Which is easier: halve margin of error or double sample size?

advanced.title: Hypothesis Tests
advanced.summary: Use null and alternative hypotheses to decide whether data look surprising.
objectives: State null and alternative hypotheses.
Interpret a test statistic as evidence scale.
Connect rejection decisions to significance level.
learn: A hypothesis test begins with a default model called the null hypothesis.
The alternative hypothesis describes the effect or difference being investigated.
A significance level sets how much false-alarm risk the procedure accepts before seeing data.
explore: Use the inference studio to shift a sample mean away from the null.
Change alpha and watch the rejection region.
Compare one-sided and two-sided evidence.
practice: Write hypotheses for testing whether a coin is fair.
Explain what alpha = 0.05 controls.
Decide whether a very ordinary sample should reject the null.
assessmentPrompts: Why do we begin with a null model?
What does rejecting the null allow us to say, and what does it not prove?

advanced.title: p-Values
advanced.summary: Read a p-value as surprise under a null model, not as the probability a claim is true.
objectives: Define p-value in context.
Avoid common p-value misinterpretations.
Relate p-values to tail areas.
learn: A p-value measures how extreme the observed result, or something more extreme, would be if the null model were true.
Small p-values are evidence against the null model.
A p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true.
explore: Use the studio distribution view to shade tail areas.
Move an observed statistic and watch the p-value change.
Compare p-values across different sample sizes.
practice: Interpret p = 0.03 in one sentence.
Say why p = 0.20 is not proof that the null is true.
Identify the tail area for a two-sided test.
assessmentPrompts: What is the reference world used to compute a p-value?
Why can a tiny effect have a small p-value in a huge sample?

advanced.title: Type I and Type II Error
advanced.summary: Balance false positives and false negatives when making statistical decisions.
objectives: Define Type I and Type II errors.
Connect alpha to false-positive risk.
Explain power as detecting real effects.
learn: A Type I error rejects a true null hypothesis.
A Type II error fails to reject a false null hypothesis.
Power is the probability of detecting an effect when the alternative is true.
explore: Use the inference studio to move the true effect and compare overlapping distributions.
Change alpha and observe the tradeoff.
Increase sample size and watch power improve.
practice: Classify a false alarm in a medical test.
Classify a missed real effect.
Explain one situation where Type I error is especially costly.
assessmentPrompts: Why can lowering alpha increase Type II error?
How does sample size help both precision and power?

advanced.title: Slope Fields
advanced.summary: Read a differential equation as a field of tiny direction instructions.
objectives: Interpret dy/dx = f(x,y) graphically.
Sketch solution curves through initial points.
Connect local slopes to global behavior.
learn: A slope field places a small segment at many points showing the derivative a solution would have there.
A solution curve threads through the field while matching the local direction.
Initial conditions select one curve from a family of possible solutions.
explore: Use the slope-fields visualizer to change f(x,y).
Move the initial point and compare solution curves.
Look for equilibrium solutions where slope is zero.
practice: Sketch a solution through (0, 1) from a simple slope field.
Identify a horizontal equilibrium in dy/dx = y(1-y).
Explain why solution curves should not cross in a well-behaved field.
assessmentPrompts: How does a slope field encode infinitely many solutions?
What role does the initial condition play?

advanced.title: Euler Method
advanced.summary: Approximate an unknown solution curve by walking along tangent directions.
objectives: Use Euler steps to approximate an IVP.
Explain the role of step size.
Compare numerical approximation with exact behavior.
learn: Euler's method starts at an initial condition and repeatedly moves by slope times step size.
Smaller steps usually improve accuracy but require more computation.
The method makes local linear predictions from the derivative.
explore: Use the differential equations studio to compare coarse and fine step sizes.
Watch error accumulate over many steps.
Try an equation where the curve bends quickly.
practice: Take two Euler steps of size 0.5 for y' = y from y(0)=1.
Explain why step size matters.
Predict when Euler's method may perform poorly.
assessmentPrompts: What information does each Euler step use?
Why is Euler's method both powerful and limited?

advanced.title: Growth and Decay IVPs
advanced.summary: Model proportional change with initial value problems and exponential solutions.
objectives: Recognize y' = ky as proportional growth or decay.
Use an initial condition to determine a solution.
Interpret k in context.
learn: When rate of change is proportional to current amount, the model is y' = ky.
Positive k gives growth and negative k gives decay.
The initial condition sets the starting amount and determines the specific exponential curve.
explore: Use the studio to vary k and the initial value.
Compare doubling and half-life interpretations.
Overlay exact curves with numerical approximations.
practice: Solve y' = 2y, y(0)=3 in formula form.
Explain what k = -0.4 means.
Find the initial value from a graph at x = 0.
assessmentPrompts: Why does proportional change lead to exponential behavior?
How is a family of solutions narrowed to one solution?

advanced.title: Logistic Differential Equation
advanced.summary: Model growth that slows as it approaches a carrying capacity.
objectives: Interpret carrying capacity.
Identify equilibria in logistic growth.
Compare logistic and exponential models.
learn: The logistic model grows nearly exponentially when the population is small.
Growth slows as the population approaches a carrying capacity.
The equilibria reveal long-run behavior without solving the equation exactly.
explore: Use the studio to change carrying capacity and growth rate.
Start above and below the carrying capacity.
Compare with y' = ky over the same interval.
practice: Identify equilibria in y' = y(1-y/10).
Explain what happens when y starts above 10.
Name one real-world limitation of logistic growth.
assessmentPrompts: Why does the logistic model bend into an S-shape?
What can equilibrium analysis tell us before solving?

advanced.title: Second-Order Oscillator
advanced.summary: Treat position, velocity, and acceleration as a coupled dynamic system.
objectives: Recognize second-order equations in motion models.
Connect y'' to acceleration.
Describe oscillation using phase behavior.
learn: A second-order differential equation involves acceleration or curvature.
The classic oscillator y'' + omega^2 y = 0 models repeated motion.
Initial position and velocity are both needed to determine a solution.
explore: Use the studio to change frequency and initial velocity.
Plot position and velocity together.
Compare undamped and damped behavior conceptually.
practice: State two initial conditions needed for a second-order IVP.
Explain what larger omega does to oscillation.
Classify y'' = -y as restoring motion.
assessmentPrompts: Why is one initial value not enough for a second-order equation?
How does the equation encode a restoring force?

advanced.title: Gamma Function
advanced.summary: Extend factorials beyond whole numbers with a continuous special function.
objectives: Use Gamma(n + 1) = n! for whole numbers.
Interpret extension beyond integers.
Identify where Gamma appears in advanced mathematics.
learn: The gamma function extends the factorial pattern to many non-integer inputs.
For positive integers, Gamma(n) = (n - 1)!.
It appears in probability distributions, integrals, and complex analysis.
explore: Use the gallery to compare factorial points with the smooth gamma curve.
Evaluate Gamma(1/2) and connect it to sqrt(pi).
Look for poles at non-positive integers.
practice: Compute Gamma(5).
State the relationship between Gamma(n) and factorial.
Name one distribution that uses Gamma.
assessmentPrompts: Why is extending factorial useful?
What makes Gamma more than curve-fitting through factorial points?

advanced.title: Beta Function
advanced.summary: Meet a two-input function that links integrals, gamma values, and distributions.
objectives: Recognize the beta function as a two-parameter integral.
Connect beta and gamma functions.
Identify its role in probability.
learn: The beta function depends on two positive parameters.
It is closely connected to gamma through B(x,y) = Gamma(x)Gamma(y)/Gamma(x+y).
It normalizes beta distributions in statistics.
explore: Use the gallery to change two parameters and observe shape changes.
Compare symmetric and skewed beta distribution shapes.
Trace how gamma values combine into beta values.
practice: Explain why a two-parameter function can control more shape than one parameter.
Use the gamma identity to simplify B(1,1).
Name one setting where values are restricted to 0 through 1.
assessmentPrompts: How does the beta function connect analysis and probability?
Why do normalizing constants matter?

advanced.title: Error Function
advanced.summary: Connect accumulated Gaussian area to probability and diffusion models.
objectives: Describe erf as an accumulated bell-curve area.
Connect erf to normal probabilities.
Recognize its role in heat and diffusion equations.
learn: The error function accumulates area under a scaled Gaussian curve.
It is closely related to the normal distribution's cumulative probability.
Its S-shape appears in diffusion, heat flow, and measurement error.
explore: Use the gallery to compare erf with a normal CDF.
Move x from negative to positive values and observe saturation.
Discuss why accumulated area produces an S-shaped curve.
practice: Describe erf(0) by symmetry.
Explain why erf approaches fixed limits far from zero.
Name one modeling context for erf.
assessmentPrompts: Why does Gaussian area matter in statistics?
How does erf translate density into cumulative probability?

advanced.title: Zeta Function
advanced.summary: Study a function whose values and zeros connect series, primes, and famous open problems.
objectives: Recognize zeta as a sum over reciprocal powers.
Connect Euler products to primes.
Relate zeta to the Riemann Hypothesis.
learn: For suitable inputs, zeta(s) sums 1/n^s over positive integers.
Euler's product formula links that sum to all prime numbers.
The function's complex zeros are central to the Riemann Hypothesis.
explore: Use the gallery to compare zeta values for different real inputs.
Connect zeta(2) with pi squared over 6.
Pair this lesson with the famous problems Riemann lesson.
practice: Explain why the series 1 + 1/2^s + 1/3^s + ... shrinks faster for larger s.
State one connection between zeta and primes.
Describe what makes zeta a special function.
assessmentPrompts: How can a series over all integers reveal information about primes?
Why is analytic continuation an important idea here?

advanced.title: Bessel Function
advanced.summary: Recognize wave-like functions that appear in circular and cylindrical symmetry.
objectives: Identify Bessel functions as special solutions to differential equations.
Connect them to radial symmetry.
Interpret zeros as physically meaningful points.
learn: Bessel functions arise when solving certain differential equations with circular or cylindrical symmetry.
Their graphs oscillate with changing amplitude.
Zeros of Bessel functions appear in vibration, waves, and boundary-value problems.
explore: Use the gallery to compare Bessel-like curves with sine waves.
Look for spacing between zeros.
Connect circular drums or waveguides to radial equations.
practice: Name one physical system where Bessel functions appear.
Describe how a Bessel graph differs from a sine wave.
Explain why symmetry changes the differential equation.
assessmentPrompts: Why do special functions often come from differential equations?
What can zeros tell us in a vibration problem?

advancedPathways.title: Number Theory Patterns
advancedPathways.summary: Move from rational approximation into famous prime and integer problems where computation suggests deep structure.
advancedPathways.outcome: Explain how examples, algorithms, and conjectures support mathematical discovery without replacing proof.
advancedPathways.capstonePrompt: Compare continued-fraction evidence for approximation with Collatz or Goldbach evidence for conjectures. Where does each kind of evidence stop?

advancedPathways.title: Inference and Modeling
advancedPathways.summary: Connect statistical decisions to dynamic models, emphasizing uncertainty, assumptions, and interpretation.
advancedPathways.outcome: Build a short argument that separates model output, sampling uncertainty, and real-world conclusions.
advancedPathways.capstonePrompt: Choose a growth or decay scenario, estimate uncertainty in a measured parameter, and explain what the model can and cannot claim.

advancedPathways.title: Special Functions and Equations
advancedPathways.summary: See special functions as named solutions, normalizers, and bridges between calculus, probability, and physics.
advancedPathways.outcome: Recognize when an advanced function is useful because it packages a recurring integral, series, or differential-equation solution.
advancedPathways.capstonePrompt: Pick Gamma, Zeta, erf, or Bessel and explain which problem type it packages: factorial extension, prime structure, Gaussian area, or symmetric waves.
